course.title: AWS Security Specialty — the Secure Workload
course.description: Secure one small AWS workload end to end: least-privilege identity proved on a denial, a segmented fenced network, data under its own keys, detection that pages, and an incident worked one change per row. Built for SCS-C03.
course.audience: Secure, defend and hand over one small AWS workload as a four-person security team — everyone runs the commands, pastes the proof and fills every record; the focus decides which record you lead.

roles.name: Identity & Access (Identity Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the identity record: users, roles, least-privilege policies and the proof of every denial.

roles.name: Infrastructure Security (Network Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the infrastructure record: the network, the segments, the security groups and the exposure.

roles.name: Data Protection (Data Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the data record: the keys, the encryption, bucket policies and what stays private.

roles.name: Detection & Response (SecOps Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the records that outlive the build: detection, the incident log, the baseline and handover.

tasks.title: Open the account and guard the spend
tasks.objective: Open the AWS free account, turn on the root MFA, and set a $1 budget alert.
definitionOfDone: The free account is open with MFA on the root user
A budget of $1 alerts by email before anything can run up a bill
The register names the account and who holds root

steps.title: Open the account and lock the root user
steps.description: The account exists, the root user has MFA, and the team agrees root is for break-glass only.
steps.instruction: Create the AWS free account for the team, turn on MFA for the root user, and then stop using root for daily work.
steps.expectedOutput: The account exists, the root user has MFA, and the team agrees root is for break-glass only.
instructionList: Use a shared team email, not a personal one.
Turn on MFA for the root user immediately; root is the one identity that can do anything.
Record that root is break-glass only; everyone works as an IAM user from Week 1.
steps.whatItMeans: Root is the account. Securing it first, and never using it again for daily work, is the first control of every AWS security baseline.

steps.title: Set a $1 budget alert from the shell
steps.description: Set a $1 budget alert from the shell
steps.instruction: Open CloudShell, confirm the account, and create a $1 monthly budget that emails the team before any spend adds up.

commands.explain: Confirms the account you are signed in to before creating anything.

commands.cmd: aws budgets describe-budgets --account-id 123456789012 2>/dev/null || echo "no budget yet — create a $1 budget in Billing"
commands.explain: Lists budgets; create the $1 alert in Billing if none exists.
commands.sample: no budget yet — create a $1 budget in Billing

steps.whatItMeans: A budget alert is the free-tier seatbelt: the email arrives long before a forgotten resource can cost real money.

outputHighlights.label: The account you are signed in to.

fixes.symptom: aws is not found in CloudShell?
fixes.fix: Open AWS CloudShell from the console top bar; the AWS CLI is built in there.
The account owner creates the $1 budget once in Billing, then everyone can read it.

tasks.title: Make an MFA identity and the CLI
tasks.objective: Create an IAM admin user with MFA for daily work, and sign the CLI in as that user, not as root.
definitionOfDone: An IAM admin user exists with MFA on
The CLI is configured to sign in as that user
The user and its MFA state are recorded in the register

steps.title: Confirm you are the IAM user, not root
steps.description: Confirm you are the IAM user, not root
steps.instruction: Configure the CLI with the IAM user’s access key, then confirm the caller is that user and not root.

commands.explain: Prints the ARN of the signed-in identity; it must be a user, not root.

steps.whatItMeans: Every command you run carries an identity. Confirming it is a scoped user, not root, is how you know a mistake has limits.

outputHighlights.label: A named IAM user, not root.

fixes.fix: You are using root access keys — delete them, make an IAM user, and configure the CLI with that user instead.

steps.title: List the account users and their MFA
steps.description: List the account users and their MFA
steps.instruction: List the IAM users and confirm the admin user has an MFA device attached.

commands.explain: Prints the MFA device serial for the user; empty means no MFA.

steps.whatItMeans: An admin user without MFA is a password away from full control. The device serial is the proof MFA is on.

outputHighlights.label: The MFA device attached to the user.

fixes.fix: Attach a virtual MFA device to the user in the IAM console, then re-run.

tasks.title: Know your team, your focus and the folder
tasks.objective: Agree who leads which record, name the workload, and make the evidence folder every artifact goes in.
definitionOfDone: Each of the four focuses has a named member
The workload has a name in the pattern sec-t<team>
The evidence folder exists with a week-0 to week-4 layout

steps.title: Pick the focus and name the workload
steps.description: Four names against four focuses, and a workload name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.instruction: Agree who leads Identity & Access, Infrastructure Security, Data Protection and Detection & Response. Name the workload sec-t and your team number.
steps.expectedOutput: Four names against four focuses, and a workload name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.whatItMeans: A focus is the record a member leads and reviews, not the only work they do. Everyone runs the commands and everyone pastes output.

steps.title: Make the evidence folder
steps.description: Make the evidence folder
steps.instruction: Create the evidence folder with a subfolder for each week. Every policy, screenshot and finding goes under the week it belongs to.

commands.explain: Five week folders in one command, then reads them back. Replace t1 with your team number.

steps.whatItMeans: An artifact nobody can find is an artifact nobody can hash. The folder is the first custody control.

tasks.title: Users, roles and MFA
tasks.objective: Give each focus a role to assume rather than a standing admin, and require MFA to assume it.
definitionOfDone: Each focus assumes a role instead of holding standing admin
The role trust policy requires MFA to assume
The matrix records who can assume what, and why

steps.title: Assume a scoped role and read the new identity
steps.description: Assume a scoped role and read the new identity
steps.instruction: Assume the focus role and confirm the temporary identity is the role, not your user.

commands.explain: Assumes the scoped role and prints the temporary role identity.

steps.whatItMeans: A role you assume gives short-lived credentials scoped to one job, which is far safer than a user who holds admin all day.

outputHighlights.label: Temporary credentials for the scoped role.

fixes.fix: The role trust policy must list your user as a principal; add it, then re-run.

steps.title: Prove the trust policy requires MFA
steps.description: Prove the trust policy requires MFA
steps.instruction: Read the role trust policy and confirm it has an MFA condition on who may assume it.

commands.explain: Prints the trust-policy conditions; an MFA condition must be present.

steps.whatItMeans: A role anyone can assume without MFA undoes the point of MFA. The condition in the trust policy is what enforces it.

outputHighlights.label: The condition that forces MFA to assume the role.

steps.title: Record the access matrix
steps.description: A matrix where every focus maps to one scoped role with a stated reason.
steps.instruction: Write the matrix: each focus, the role it assumes, what that role may do, and why it needs it.
steps.expectedOutput: A matrix where every focus maps to one scoped role with a stated reason.
steps.whatItMeans: The matrix is what an auditor reads to see that access matches need. Without it, least privilege is a claim, not a record.

handoff.note: Your section of the Identity & Access Matrix, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Least privilege, proved on a denial
tasks.objective: Write the smallest policy a role needs, then prove with the simulator that it allows the intended action and denies the forbidden one.
definitionOfDone: The policy grants only the actions the role needs
The simulator allows the intended action
The simulator denies an action the role must not do, and the denial is recorded

steps.title: Prove the intended action is allowed
steps.description: Prove the intended action is allowed
steps.instruction: Run the policy simulator for the action the role should be able to do, and read the allowed decision.

commands.explain: Asks IAM whether the role may do the action; prints the decision.

steps.whatItMeans: The simulator answers the real question — what can this identity actually do — without touching any resource.

outputHighlights.label: The intended action is permitted.

steps.title: Prove the forbidden action is denied
steps.description: Prove the forbidden action is denied
steps.instruction: Run the simulator for an action the role must not do, and confirm it is denied. This is the proof least privilege holds.

commands.cmd: aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/data-reader --action-names s3:DeleteObject iam:CreateUser --query "EvaluationResults[].[EvalActionName,EvalDecision]" --output text
commands.explain: Checks two forbidden actions; both must come back denied.

steps.whatItMeans: A permission you never proved is denied is a permission you are only hoping is denied. The denial is the control, and the record of it is the evidence.

outputHighlights.label: The forbidden actions are refused.

fixes.symptom: A forbidden action came back allowed?
fixes.fix: A broader policy is granting it. Narrow the policy or add an explicit deny, then re-run until it denies.

handoff.note: Your section of the Identity & Access Matrix, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: The account governance baseline
tasks.objective: Turn on the account-wide controls that make everything else auditable: a trail of every call, and a config recorder.
definitionOfDone: A multi-region CloudTrail is logging and recorded
Config is recording resource changes, or its absence is justified
The baseline lists each control and whether it is on

steps.title: Confirm a trail is logging every call
steps.description: Confirm a trail is logging every call
steps.instruction: List the CloudTrail trails and confirm one is multi-region and logging.

commands.explain: Lists the trails and whether each is multi-region.

steps.whatItMeans: CloudTrail is the record of who did what. Without a multi-region trail, an action in a quiet region leaves no footprint.

outputHighlights.label: The trail covers every region.

fixes.fix: Create a multi-region trail to an S3 bucket in the console, then re-run.

steps.title: Confirm the trail log file is validated
steps.description: Confirm the trail log file is validated
steps.instruction: Confirm log-file validation is on, so a tampered log can be detected.

commands.cmd: aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name org-trail --query "IsLogging" --output text && aws cloudtrail describe-trails --query "trailList[?Name=='org-trail'].LogFileValidationEnabled" --output text
commands.explain: Confirms the trail is logging and that log-file validation is enabled.

steps.whatItMeans: Log-file validation is what lets you prove the trail was not edited after the fact. A log you cannot trust is not evidence.

outputHighlights.label: Logging on and log files validated.

handoff.note: Your section of the Control Baseline, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: The segmented network
tasks.objective: Read the network as segments — a public subnet for what faces the world, a private one for what must not.
definitionOfDone: The VPC has a public and a private subnet, recorded
The private subnet has no direct route to the internet gateway
The segmentation is drawn in the record

steps.title: List the subnets and whether they are public
steps.description: List the subnets and whether they are public
steps.instruction: List the subnets in the VPC and whether each auto-assigns a public IP, which marks it public.

commands.explain: Lists each subnet and whether it is public (true) or private (false).

steps.whatItMeans: Segmentation is the first network control: what faces the world sits in the public subnet, and the data sits in the private one, with no public IP.

outputHighlights.label: The private subnet assigns no public IP.

fixes.fix: Your private subnet is public. Turn off auto-assign public IP and route it through a NAT, not the internet gateway.

steps.title: Prove the private subnet has no door to the internet
steps.description: Prove the private subnet has no door to the internet
steps.instruction: Read the private subnet route table and confirm no route points at the internet gateway.

commands.explain: Lists the gateways the private subnet routes to; an igw- here would be a leak.

steps.whatItMeans: A private subnet whose route table points at an internet gateway is not private. The route table is where segmentation is really enforced.

outputHighlights.label: Only the local route — no path to the internet gateway.

handoff.note: Your section of the Network Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Least-exposure security groups
tasks.objective: Open only the one port the service needs, and prove with a dry-run that a wider rule would be refused.
definitionOfDone: The security group opens only the needed port to the needed source
No rule opens a port to 0.0.0.0/0 that should not be public
A dry-run of a too-wide rule is recorded as refused or flagged

steps.title: Find any rule open to the whole internet
steps.description: Find any rule open to the whole internet
steps.instruction: List the ingress rules and flag any that allow 0.0.0.0/0, the open-to-the-world source.

commands.explain: Prints the port ranges any rule opens to the whole internet; empty is best.

steps.whatItMeans: A security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 is the most common cloud finding there is. Only a port that is meant to be public, like 443, belongs there.

outputHighlights.label: Only HTTPS is open to the world — SSH must not appear here.

fixes.fix: Remove that rule. Reach the host through SSM in the next task, not an open management port.

steps.title: Dry-run a too-wide rule to prove it is caught
steps.description: Dry-run a too-wide rule to prove it is caught
steps.instruction: Attempt to add an SSH-from-anywhere rule with --dry-run, so nothing changes but the attempt is tested.

commands.cmd: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0abc --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0 --dry-run 2>&1 | head -1
commands.explain: Tests the dangerous rule without applying it; the dry-run message shows it would have run, so your review, not AWS, is the gate.
commands.sample: An error occurred (DryRunOperation) when calling the AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress operation: Request would have succeeded, but DryRun flag is set.

steps.expectedOutput: An error occurred (DryRunOperation) when calling the AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress operation: Request would have succeeded, but DryRun flag is set.
steps.whatItMeans: A dry-run lets you test a change without making it. The lesson: AWS will happily open SSH to the world, so the control is your review and your group policy, not the API.

outputHighlights.label: The change was tested, not applied.

handoff.note: Your section of the Network Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Reach the host without opening SSH
tasks.objective: Reach the private host through Systems Manager Session Manager, so port 22 can stay closed to everyone.
definitionOfDone: The host is reachable through SSM with no inbound SSH rule
The SSM session is logged
The record shows port 22 closed and the session audited

steps.title: Confirm the host is managed by SSM
steps.description: Confirm the host is managed by SSM
steps.instruction: List the SSM-managed instances and confirm the host appears Online, which means you can reach it without SSH.

commands.explain: Lists instances SSM can manage and whether each is reachable.

steps.whatItMeans: An instance SSM can reach is an instance you never need to open SSH to. The management path moves off the network and onto an audited API.

outputHighlights.label: The host is reachable through SSM.

fixes.fix: Attach an instance role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore and make sure the SSM agent is running, then re-run.

steps.title: Confirm no inbound SSH remains
steps.description: Confirm no inbound SSH remains
steps.instruction: Confirm the host’s security group has no inbound rule on port 22 at all.

commands.cmd: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-0abc --query "SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions[?FromPort==`22`]" --output text; echo "exit scan: $?"
commands.explain: Prints any port-22 rule; an empty result means SSH is fully closed.

steps.whatItMeans: The whole point of SSM is that port 22 can be closed to everyone. An empty port-22 result is the proof the door is gone, not just guarded.

handoff.note: Your section of the Network Security Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: A customer-managed key
tasks.objective: Create a customer-managed KMS key with a key policy, and encrypt the data with it rather than an AWS-managed key.
definitionOfDone: A customer-managed key exists with a key policy, recorded
The key policy grants use to only the roles that need it
The data is encrypted with the key, proved

steps.title: Confirm the key is customer-managed
steps.description: Confirm the key is customer-managed
steps.instruction: Read the key and confirm its manager is the customer, not AWS, which is what lets you control the policy and rotation.

commands.explain: Prints who manages the key and whether it is enabled.

steps.whatItMeans: A customer-managed key is one you set the policy on and can rotate and disable. An AWS-managed key gives you none of that control.

outputHighlights.label: The key is yours to govern.

fixes.fix: You are reading an AWS-managed key. Create a customer-managed key and an alias, then re-run against the alias.

steps.title: Prove the data object is encrypted with your key
steps.description: Prove the data object is encrypted with your key
steps.instruction: Read an object’s encryption and confirm it is SSE-KMS with your key, not the default.

commands.cmd: aws s3api head-object --bucket sec-t1-data --key report.csv --query "[ServerSideEncryption,SSEKMSKeyId]" --output text
commands.explain: Prints the object’s encryption type and the key id used.

steps.whatItMeans: Encryption at rest is only as controlled as the key behind it. SSE-KMS with your key means you, not AWS alone, decide who can decrypt.

outputHighlights.label: The object is encrypted with a KMS key.

handoff.note: Your section of the Data Protection Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: The locked, encrypted bucket
tasks.objective: Block public access on the bucket and make it refuse an unencrypted upload, so data cannot land in the clear.
definitionOfDone: Block Public Access is fully on for the bucket
The bucket policy denies an unencrypted put
An unencrypted upload is shown being refused

steps.title: Confirm public access is fully blocked
steps.description: Confirm public access is fully blocked
steps.instruction: Read the bucket’s public-access block and confirm all four settings are true.

commands.explain: Prints the four block-public-access flags; all must be true.

steps.whatItMeans: A public S3 bucket is the headline breach. Block Public Access set fully on is the one control that makes an accidental public grant impossible.

outputHighlights.label: The last of the four blocks — all on.

fixes.fix: Turn Block Public Access fully on at the bucket, and at the account level too, then re-run.

steps.title: Prove an unencrypted upload is refused
steps.description: Prove an unencrypted upload is refused
steps.instruction: Try to put an object without encryption and confirm the bucket policy denies it.

commands.cmd: aws s3api put-object --bucket sec-t1-data --key test.txt --body test.txt 2>&1 | head -1; echo "---"; aws s3api put-object --bucket sec-t1-data --key test.txt --body test.txt --server-side-encryption aws:kms 2>&1 | grep -o ETag | head -1
commands.explain: The first put (no encryption) is denied; the second (with KMS) succeeds.
commands.sample:
An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the PutObject operation: ... s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption
---
ETag

steps.expectedOutput:
An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the PutObject operation: ... s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption
---
ETag
steps.whatItMeans: A bucket that accepts an unencrypted object is a bucket where someone will eventually land data in the clear. The deny-unencrypted policy makes that impossible.

outputHighlights.label: The unencrypted upload was refused.

handoff.note: Your section of the Data Protection Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Read what detection found
tasks.objective: Read a set of detection findings, sort them by severity, and decide which one is the incident to work.
prerequisites: The sample findings file shipped with the course (findings.json)
definitionOfDone: The findings are listed by severity, highest first
The highest-severity finding is identified as the incident to work
The triage is recorded with the finding type and severity

steps.title: Sort the findings by severity
steps.description: Sort the findings by severity
steps.instruction: Read the sample findings file and sort them so the most severe is first. No paid service is needed — the findings are provided.

commands.explain: Sorts the shipped findings by severity, highest first, and prints severity and type.

steps.whatItMeans: Detection without triage is just noise. Sorting by severity is the first move: it says which finding is the fire and which is the smoke.

outputHighlights.label: The highest-severity finding — the incident to work.

fixes.fix: Install jq from your package manager; it ships in AWS CloudShell already.

steps.title: Pull the detail of the top finding
steps.description: Pull the detail of the top finding
steps.instruction: Read the full detail of the highest-severity finding, so the incident log opens with the facts.

commands.explain: Prints the type, the actor and the source IP of the top finding.

steps.whatItMeans: The incident starts from the finding’s own facts: who, from where, doing what. That is the symptom you write down before any theory.

outputHighlights.label: The finding type that names the incident.

handoff.note: Your section of the Detection & Findings Log, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Work the incident with the runbook
tasks.objective: Work the top finding as an incident the method way: one theory, one containment action, one result per row, until it is contained.
prerequisites: The top finding from the detection log (Week 3)
definitionOfDone: The incident is written exactly, before any action
Every step is a row: theory, the one action, the result
At least one action did not contain it and the row says so
The incident is contained and the lesson is recorded

steps.title: Write the incident exactly
steps.description: The log opens with the actor, the source IP, the unauthorized action and why it is an incident, and no acti…
steps.instruction: Before any action, write what happened from the finding: the actor, the source, the action, and why it is an incident.
steps.expectedOutput: The log opens with the actor, the source IP, the unauthorized action and why it is an incident, and no action yet.
steps.whatItMeans: The method starts with the incident written down. For a cloud incident the symptom is the exact finding — actor, source, action — not a feeling that something is off.

steps.title: Contain it one action per row
steps.description: Contain it one action per row
steps.instruction: Write one theory for how to contain it, take exactly one action, and record the result. An action that does not contain it gets its own row.

commands.cmd: aws iam update-access-key --user-name secops --access-key-id AKIAEXAMPLE --status Inactive && aws iam get-access-key-last-used --access-key-id AKIAEXAMPLE --query "AccessKeyLastUsed.Region" --output text && echo "key disabled"
commands.explain: Disables the compromised access key, then confirms the change. This is the first containment action.

steps.whatItMeans: One action per row is what makes the incident log trustworthy: you can always say which action contained it. The same method A+ uses on hardware.

outputHighlights.label: The compromised credential is contained.

fixes.symptom: Disabling the key did not stop it?
fixes.fix: The actor may hold a session token too. Next row: revoke active sessions by attaching an AWSRevokeOlderSessions policy, one change, and re-check.

steps.title: Record containment and the lesson
steps.description: The log ends contained, keeps every action that failed, and names the preventive change.
steps.instruction: Write that the incident is contained, keep the rows for the actions that did not work, and record the one change that stops it recurring.
steps.expectedOutput: The log ends contained, keeps every action that failed, and names the preventive change.
steps.whatItMeans: A log with no failed actions in it is a log nobody believes. The lesson — the change that stops the next one — is what turns an incident into an improvement.

handoff.note: Your section of the Incident Response Log, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Wire the detection alarm
tasks.objective: Wire a metric filter and alarm so the next unauthorized call pages the team instead of waiting to be found.
definitionOfDone: A metric filter matches the unauthorized pattern in the trail logs
An alarm on the metric notifies the team
The alarm is shown in OK or configured state

steps.title: Confirm the metric filter matches the pattern
steps.description: Confirm the metric filter matches the pattern
steps.instruction: List the metric filters on the trail log group and confirm one matches unauthorized or denied calls.

commands.explain: Lists the metric filters and their patterns; one should match AccessDenied / UnauthorizedOperation.

steps.whatItMeans: A metric filter turns a line in the trail into a number you can alarm on. It is how a detective control becomes an alert instead of a log nobody reads.

outputHighlights.label: The filter that counts denied and unauthorized calls.

fixes.fix: Create one on the CloudTrail log group with the AccessDenied / UnauthorizedOperation pattern, then re-run.

steps.title: Confirm the alarm will notify
steps.description: Confirm the alarm will notify
steps.instruction: Read the alarm on that metric and confirm it has an action, so it pages rather than just turning red.

commands.explain: Prints the alarm state and its first action; an SNS topic ARN means it notifies.

steps.whatItMeans: An alarm with no action just changes colour on a dashboard nobody is watching. The notification action is what makes detection reach a human.

outputHighlights.label: The alarm notifies a topic the team subscribes to.

handoff.note: Your section of the Detection & Findings Log, for the review that approves it.

prerequisites: Every other record of the course, filled
definitionOfDone: The baseline lists every control and whether it is on
Each open risk has an owner and a mitigation
Every artifact has a custody row with its hash

steps.title: Write the control baseline and the open risks
steps.description: A one-page baseline a new team could run from, with every control’s state and every open risk owned.
steps.instruction: Write the baseline in one page by reference to the other records: identity, network, data, detection — each control, on or off, and each open risk with an owner.
steps.expectedOutput: A one-page baseline a new team could run from, with every control’s state and every open risk owned.
steps.whatItMeans: The baseline is the document the next security team reads before touching the workload. Written honestly, it says exactly what is protected and what is not yet.

DOMAINS.label: Technical capability
DOMAINS.definition: Skills, tools, commands and exam domains proven by pasted output that held every expected token.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the commands the job needs?
DOMAINS.evidence: A verification record per step: the output hash, the tokens matched, the attempts, and a receipt in cloud mode.

DOMAINS.label: Professional execution
DOMAINS.definition: Procedures followed to standard, steps in order, first pastes, evidence named, checks met, documents controlled, work on time.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and deliver on the calendar?
DOMAINS.evidence: The order of verification stamps, the attempts, the file names, the Definition-of-Done checks, the control block and the cohort due dates.

DOMAINS.label: Problem solving
DOMAINS.definition: Faults logged and resolved, steps verified after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes from first paste to proof.
DOMAINS.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?
DOMAINS.evidence: Fault, incident and triage rows with their outcome column, retries that verified, the append-only flag history and two stamps per step.

DOMAINS.label: Thought process
DOMAINS.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options with rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback, and reasons written on change rows.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?
DOMAINS.evidence: Decision blocks with the option chosen, who chose it and when, the answers to the supporting questions, and the form lifecycle.

DOMAINS.label: Architecture and design
DOMAINS.definition: Design briefs, topologies, IP plans, bills of materials, decision records and as-built documents drafted, approved and issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member design a system and write it down so another team can build it?
DOMAINS.evidence: The architecture and configuration forms of the role: rows filled, checks met, approved or issued, with the decisions on them.

DOMAINS.label: Team and communication
DOMAINS.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given, steps ticked for teammates, reports filed, notes written, handovers issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly, review others and hold their lane?
DOMAINS.evidence: The lifecycle rows with who moved what, the hand-offs and their forms, the peer review queue, the reports and the notes.

DOMAINS.label: Learning and retention
DOMAINS.definition: Skills proved on a second task, verified again a week or more later, reused in another course, and the pace month on month.
DOMAINS.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?
DOMAINS.evidence: The verification stamps of every skill: first and last, the tasks and courses between them, and the last two months of them.

DOMAINS.label: Professional readiness
DOMAINS.definition: The tier per record item at ten verified uses, the exam weight verified, the work-role coverage and the readiness score.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member consistently perform at a professional level in a real work environment?
DOMAINS.evidence: Every category of the record with its verified uses across courses, the published exam weights and the work roles’ required competencies.

KPIS.label: Skills verified
KPIS.numerator: Skills with at least one step verified from pasted output.
KPIS.denominator: Skills the role practises that carry a verifiable step.
KPIS.whyMember: Each verified skill names a task where the pasted output held every expected token.
KPIS.whyCompany: Skills backed by matched output rather than a tick, with the task behind each one named.

KPIS.label: Exam weight verified
KPIS.numerator: The published exam weight of every domain with a verified step, summed.
KPIS.denominator: The published exam weight of every domain the role practises, summed.
KPIS.whyMember: Shows which share of the exam blueprint the verified work already touches.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reads the verified work against the published exam domains and their weights.

KPIS.label: Commands verified
KPIS.numerator: Verified required steps that run a command.
KPIS.denominator: Verifiable required steps that run a command.
KPIS.whyMember: Command steps proven by their output; the table below splits them by tool.
KPIS.whyCompany: Tool use proven by output, per command step, split by tool in the table.

KPIS.label: Procedures to standard
KPIS.numerator: Followed procedures whose form cites a control code and was approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Procedures followed: every check due met and document control complete.
KPIS.whyMember: A runbook followed to a named control and approved by the team; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Procedures run to a cited NIST, ISO or SOC 2 control and approved by the team.

KPIS.label: Faults resolved
KPIS.numerator: Fault, incident and triage rows whose outcome column reads resolved.
KPIS.denominator: Fault, incident and triage rows the team filled on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every fault the team logged, and how many ended resolved; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Troubleshooting success read from the fault and incident records the team kept.

KPIS.label: Verified after retry
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps that took more than one paste.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: A step that failed once and was then proven: the fault was found and fixed.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often a failed first paste was followed by a verified fix.

KPIS.label: Stuck flags cleared
KPIS.numerator: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared.
KPIS.denominator: Stuck flags the member raised.
KPIS.whyMember: Asking for help and then getting past it both count; a flag never cleared says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Blockers raised and worked through, from the append-only flag history.

KPIS.label: Time to resolution
KPIS.numerator: The median minutes from the first paste to the verification, per verified step with both stamps.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps with both stamps; the share within the hour is the percentage.
KPIS.whyMember: The median, so one long gap moves nothing; a step left over a day is counted apart.
KPIS.whyCompany: Minutes from first attempt to proof, read from two recorded stamps, never a clock.

KPIS.label: Steps verified in order
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose verifiable steps were verified in the authored order.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with two or more verification records, so an order exists.
KPIS.whyMember: The procedure was run as written, step after step.
KPIS.whyCompany: Runbooks followed in order, read from the sequence of verification records.

KPIS.label: First-try verifications
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps whose first paste held every expected token.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: Shown beside retries: a step verified after several pastes counts for as much.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often the first paste matched, printed beside how often it took more than one.

KPIS.label: Files named to convention
KPIS.numerator: Hashed files named to the evidence convention.
KPIS.denominator: Hashed files.
KPIS.whyMember: Evidence an auditor can find: date, team, tool and subject in every file name.
KPIS.whyCompany: Chain-of-custody hygiene: hashed files that follow the naming convention.

KPIS.label: Definition-of-Done met
KPIS.numerator: Definition-of-Done checks met on the forms of the role.
KPIS.denominator: Checks due on those forms through the current week.
KPIS.whyMember: Every check a form must pass this week, met or not, counted for the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Work products measured against their own acceptance checks, week by week.

KPIS.label: Decisions recorded
KPIS.numerator: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member.
KPIS.denominator: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.
KPIS.whyMember: Each decision names the options weighed, the one chosen, who chose and when.
KPIS.whyCompany: Component, configuration and architecture choices made against named alternatives.

KPIS.label: Decisions justified
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: A choice with its reason, the rejected options and the risk accepted.
KPIS.whyCompany: Judgment shown in writing: rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback per decision.

KPIS.label: Decisions approved
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: The team stood behind the choice; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Decisions that passed the team’s review and were issued.

KPIS.label: Changes with rollback
KPIS.numerator: Change-record rows with a rollback or back-out written.
KPIS.denominator: Change-record rows on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every change the team logged, and how many had a way back written down first.
KPIS.whyCompany: Change discipline: a rollback plan on every recorded change.

KPIS.label: Hand-offs completed
KPIS.numerator: Hand-offs whose named deliverable reached approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Hand-offs of the tasks of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Work handed to another role that the team then approved or issued.
KPIS.whyCompany: Cross-role hand-offs closed by an approved document.

KPIS.label: RACI respected
KPIS.numerator: Lifecycle moves the member made in the role the RACI names for that move.
KPIS.denominator: Lifecycle moves the member made on forms with a RACI.
KPIS.whyMember: Submitting as the drafter, approving as the approver: the lane was held.
KPIS.whyCompany: Role discipline on documents, read from who moved what.

KPIS.label: Peer reviews given
KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked
KPIS.numerator: Required steps the member ticked on another role’s tasks.
KPIS.denominator: No denominator: a count.
KPIS.whyMember: Steps done on a teammate’s task, so a lane short of hands still finished.
KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.
KPIS.whyMember: The due date comes from the cohort calendar; without one the row says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

KPIS.label: Values recalled
KPIS.numerator: Recall activities answered correctly: the value the team recorded, picked among distractors.
KPIS.denominator: Recall activities answered, from the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Weeks after recording an address, a prefix, a port or a decision, the member still knows it.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention of the project the member built, read from answers given without the form open.

KPIS.label: Scenarios applied
KPIS.numerator: Applied scenarios answered correctly: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size.
KPIS.denominator: Applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Takes a value the team recorded and uses it under a change the course did not script.
KPIS.whyCompany: Applied use of recorded facts, not recall alone; offered scenarios count whether or not answered.

KPIS.label: Conflicts resolved
KPIS.numerator: Conflicts the record found that the team resolved: the address, the port, the prefix, the size no longer at odds.
KPIS.denominator: Conflicts the record found at the checkpoints reached, resolved or still open.
KPIS.whyMember: A duplicate address or an over-committed host found by the platform and fixed by the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Contradictions in the record closed, read from the record itself rather than from a claim.

KPIS.label: Minutes on task
KPIS.numerator: Whole minutes the member had tasks of this course open on a visible tab, pauses excluded.
KPIS.denominator: A count; nothing is read into it.
KPIS.whyMember: How long the work took the member, by the timer they can pause; measured, never rewarded.
KPIS.whyCompany: Time on task as context for the other rows; no score reads it.

METRICS.label: RACI respected

METRICS.label: Peer reviews given

METRICS.label: Stuck flags helped

METRICS.label: Partial progress
METRICS.definition: Verifiable steps with some tokens matched and not verified, over verifiable steps.

METRICS.label: Reports filed

METRICS.label: Notes written

METRICS.label: Independence
METRICS.definition: Steps verified with no stuck flag ever raised, over verified steps.

METRICS.label: Active days

METRICS.label: Active weeks

METRICS.label: Retention

METRICS.label: Profile coverage

PRACTICES.label: Least privilege
PRACTICES.definition: Every account, role and agent holds only the rights its task needs, and nothing it might need later.

PRACTICES.label: Defence in depth
PRACTICES.definition: More than one control stands between an attacker and the asset, so one failure is not a breach.

PRACTICES.label: Default deny
PRACTICES.definition: Nothing passes a boundary unless a rule allows it; the allow list is the policy.

PRACTICES.label: Periodic access review
PRACTICES.definition: Accounts and rights are reviewed on a schedule; orphans are disabled and the review is recorded.

PRACTICES.label: Hash evidence at capture
PRACTICES.definition: Every artifact is hashed when it is saved and the digest is recorded, so later copies can be checked.

PRACTICES.label: Authorised testing only
PRACTICES.definition: Scanning and attacks happen inside a signed scope and rules of engagement, against the pod the team owns.

PRACTICES.label: Retest to closure
PRACTICES.definition: A finding is closed only by a retest that shows the fix, and every finding ends Closed, Open or Risk accepted.

PRACTICES.label: Hardening baseline
PRACTICES.definition: Hosts are configured to a written benchmark and checked against it, so drift from the baseline is visible.

PRACTICES.label: Guardrail regression tests
PRACTICES.definition: Every blocked attack case becomes a test the pipeline runs, so a removed guardrail fails the build.

PRACTICES.label: Right-sizing
PRACTICES.definition: Resources are sized from measured use, reviewed and shrunk when the measurement says so.

PRACTICES.label: Centralised logging
PRACTICES.definition: Every host ships its logs to one place where they are kept, searched and alerted on.

PRACTICES.label: Alert to ticket
PRACTICES.definition: A detection opens a ticket with an owner and a due time, so nothing fires into silence.

PRACTICES.label: Detection as code
PRACTICES.definition: Detections are written as versioned rules, mapped to a technique id and validated against a test attack.

PRACTICES.label: Contain before analysing
PRACTICES.definition: An active attacker is blocked and the block is timestamped before the deeper analysis begins.

PRACTICES.label: As-built documentation
PRACTICES.definition: What was actually built is recorded, with addresses, versions and owners, and handed over with the system.

PRACTICES.label: Data classification
PRACTICES.definition: Information is classified on a written scale, and handling rules follow the class.

PRACTICES.label: Control mapping
PRACTICES.definition: Each control is mapped to the criteria it satisfies across frameworks, with an owner and an evidence source.

PRACTICES.label: Corrective action
PRACTICES.definition: Every nonconformity gets a cause, a corrective action, an owner and a date, and the action is checked.

PRACTICES.label: Customer assurance
PRACTICES.definition: A customer question is answered with evidence or an honest gap, never with a promise.

PRACTICES.label: Input and output guardrails
PRACTICES.definition: Prompts and model outputs pass through filters that block or contain the listed attack cases.

PRACTICES.label: Human checkpoint
PRACTICES.definition: AI-assisted work passes a named human check before it is acted on, and the check is recorded.

PRACTICES.label: Suites with a pass line
PRACTICES.definition: An attack or evaluation suite states what passing means before it runs.

PRACTICES.label: Encryption at rest
PRACTICES.definition: Stored data, snapshots and backups are encrypted under a managed key, and nothing is shared or public.

SCORING.label: Tool proficiency
SCORING.definition: Commands and skills proven by output, and skills proved on a second task, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Reads browser checks and receipts of stamps, not proof of the machine; the per-tool table names each command.

SCORING.label: Troubleshooting success
SCORING.definition: Faults resolved, retries that verified, stuck flags cleared and steps resolved within the hour, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Faults are team rows; the minutes are a median between two recorded stamps, so a step left open overnight is counted apart.

SCORING.label: Judgment
SCORING.definition: Decisions recorded, justified and approved, and changes with a rollback written, equally weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Counts what was written against named options; it does not judge whether the choice was right.

SCORING.label: Collaboration
SCORING.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected and peer reviews given, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Team facts count for the team; the role share on the KPIs says what this member moved.

SCORING.label: Reliability
SCORING.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, document control complete, controls cited and instructor approval, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: On time needs the cohort start date; without one the score stands on the other three and says so.

SCORING.label: Readiness
SCORING.definition: Exam weight verified, work-role coverage, skills retained and steps in order, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: A reading of the record against an exam and a work role, not a prediction of a pass or a hire.

SCORING.label: Understanding retained
SCORING.definition: Values recalled, scenarios applied and conflicts resolved, weeks after the team recorded them, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Asks only about values the team recorded; before the checkpoint week the score stands on nothing and says so.

SOPS.label: Incident response plan
SOPS.definition: The written plan for handling an incident: roles, the first hour, containment, communication and the notice deadline.

SOPS.label: Chain of custody
SOPS.definition: Every evidence item logged with its hash, who held it, when, and where it is stored.

SOPS.label: Hardening baseline
SOPS.definition: The settings a host must have, the benchmark they come from, and the proof each host meets them.

SOPS.label: Operational handover

SOPS.label: Data handling standard

SOPS.label: Access review

SOPS.label: Detection rules

SOPS.label: Asset inventory

SOPS.label: Control mapping

SOPS.label: Network design
